extracted.intended_audience: Stanford CS103 students / undergraduate CS students learning proof-writing
extracted.subtask_description: A short, structured guide for writing clear mathematical proofs in an undergraduate CS course, organized by the kind of statement being proved (implications, quantifiers, biconditionals, contraposition, contradiction). Emphasizes explicit signposting of each proof step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proofs of implications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these steps: 1) "Clearly state to your reader that you are assuming the antecedent is true." 2) State you will prove the consequent. 3) Provide reasoning connecting assumption to conclusion. 4) "Indicate to the reader that you ended up where you said you were going." Emphasizes explicit announcement of assumption and an explicit concluding signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universally-quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern for proving statements of the form 'for all x, P(x)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) "Instruct the reader to pick an arbitrary object" — use words like "Pick", "Consider", "Let", "Fix", or "Choose." 2) Prove the object necessarily has the required property. 3) Provide the logical reasoning. 4) Confirm the stated goal was achieved. Emphasizes choosing an arbitrary element and showing the property holds generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existentially-quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern for proving statements of the form 'there exists x such that P(x)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key difference from universal proofs: tell the reader which object you're picking. Structure: 1) Specify the exact object satisfying the requirement. 2) Demonstrate it possesses all necessary properties. Implicit guidance: give a concrete witness and verify each needed property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: How to prove statements of the form 'P if and only if Q'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Write out two separate proofs, one for each of the two implications." That is, prove P => Q and Q => P separately, each following an appropriate proof pattern (e.g., direct, contrapositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure for proving an implication by proving its contrapositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Announce "I will prove the contrapositive." 2) Write out the contrapositive explicitly. 3) Prove the contrapositive using any standard technique. Emphasizes explicit metalinguistic signaling that the contrapositive is being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure for proofs that assume the negation and derive an impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) "Assume that X is false" and "explicitly write out the negation." 2) Derive an impossible conclusion. 3) "State that you've reached a contradiction." 4) Conclude the original assumption was incorrect. Emphasizes writing the negation explicitly, deriving contradiction, and clearly announcing the contradiction and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good math-writing (signposting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-guideline about the style and presentation of proofs used throughout the rubric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CS103 rubric is explicitly metalinguistic: every proof signposts what kind of proof it is and where in the structure each step sits. A "good" proof in this register is one in which every move is announced. Practical implications: always tell the reader what you will assume, what you will prove, when you switch techniques (e.g., "I will prove the contrapositive"), and when you have finished a subproof.
